title: Searching: linear search and binary search; preconditions
learningObjectives: Implement linear search and explain why it works on both sorted and unsorted sequences.
Implement iterative binary search using a clearly defined half-open interval.
State and verify the sorted-input precondition required by binary search.
Compare best- and worst-case comparison counts for linear and binary search.
Handle empty arrays, absent keys, duplicate keys and index-result representation safely.
Test search functions with boundary cases and explain the meaning of a not-found result.

understand.concept: Searching locates a target value or determines that it is absent. Linear search checks elements one by one and works without an ordering precondition. Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted search interval, reducing the remaining candidates quickly when its sortedness precondition is satisfied.
understand.whyItMatters: The fastest algorithm is not useful if its preconditions are false. Linear search is simple and works on unsorted data; binary search is efficient for sorted data but can return incorrect results if the ordering assumption is not met.
understand.analogy: Linear search is like checking every name in a paper list. Binary search is like opening a sorted directory near the middle and deciding which half can still contain the name.
understand.analogyLimit: Binary search's halving strategy depends on a consistent ordering and random access to the sequence. It is not a shortcut for searching arbitrary unsorted data or a singly linked list.

explain.narrative:
For linear search, begin at index zero and compare each element with the target. Stop on a match or after count elements. Its worst-case number of comparisons is proportional to n; the best case is one comparison when the first element matches. It needs no sorting.

For binary search, require that the array is sorted in the same order used by the comparison. Use a half-open interval [low, high): low is included and high is excluded. While low < high, compute mid = low + (high - low) / 2. If a[mid] is smaller than the target, set low = mid + 1; otherwise set high = mid. When the loop ends, low is the lower-bound insertion position; check low < count and a[low] == target before reporting a match. This form returns the first matching position when duplicates exist.

Use size_t for array positions and a separate success result rather than narrowing an arbitrary index to int. Define the contract for a null pointer and nonzero count. Test empty, one-element, first, last, missing and duplicate targets. Binary search has logarithmic worst-case comparisons, while linear search is linear; for tiny or frequently changing data, the simpler linear approach may still be appropriate.

examples.title: Linear search with a separate success result
examples.explanation: The function scans each element and stores the matching index only on success. It returns false for an absent target or invalid output pointer. An empty array with count zero is a valid search that returns false.

examples.title: Binary search returns the first matching position
examples.explanation: The half-open interval shrinks until low is the first index whose value is not less than target. The final equality check confirms a match. The caller must provide an array sorted in ascending order; the function cannot verify that precondition cheaply on every call.

practise.guidedTask: Trace both algorithms on [2, 4, 7, 9, 12, 15] when searching for 9 and then 8. Record every comparison and each low/high/mid update for binary search.
practise.independentTask: Implement both searches for an array of integers. Test empty input, one element, duplicates, absent targets and first/last positions. Add a written precondition to the binary-search function and explain why the same code is invalid for unsorted data.
hints: Linear search does not require sorted input.
Binary search requires the data to be sorted under the comparison it uses.
A half-open interval [low, high) excludes high.
Use low + (high - low) / 2 for a safe midpoint calculation.
Do not convert size_t indices to int without a representability guarantee.
Specify whether duplicate matches return any occurrence or the first occurrence.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm can search an unsorted array without first sorting it?
questions.explanation: Linear search checks elements without relying on an ordering.

questions.prompt: What is the essential precondition for ordinary binary search?
options: The sequence is sorted according to the comparison used
The array length must be a power of two
questions.answer: The sequence is sorted according to the comparison used
questions.explanation: Binary search eliminates a half based on ordering; without sorted order that elimination is unsound.

questions.prompt: In a half-open interval [low, high), is high a valid candidate index?
questions.explanation: The interval includes low through high - 1.

questions.prompt: Why compute mid as low + (high - low) / 2?
options: It avoids potentially overflowing the addition low + high
questions.answer: It avoids potentially overflowing the addition low + high
questions.explanation: The difference is bounded by the interval, avoiding a potentially overflowing sum.

questions.prompt: A sorted array contains three copies of the target. How can binary search be designed to return the first?
options: Continue narrowing toward the lower bound and check equality at the final position
Return immediately on the first equality encountered
questions.answer: Continue narrowing toward the lower bound and check equality at the final position
questions.explanation: Lower-bound search continues into the left side after equality to find the first matching index.
